Wrinkle
RING-kl
n. (a crease or fold; a mark of age or wear)
Greek rhutis, a wrinkle or fold in cloth or skin. Old English wrinclian, to wind about. Paul pairs it with spot to describe what the church will not have when Christ presents her to himself.

Biblical Definition

That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. The verse states the purpose of Christ's love for the church, and the whole sentence is about what he does. He loved the church and gave himself for it; he sanctifies and cleanses it; he presents it to himself. The bride contributes nothing to her own adorning. Spot and wrinkle are drawn from cloth and from skin, and the pair covers both kinds of fault — the stain that comes from outside and the crease that comes from age and use. Neither will be found. The word present is a wedding word, and glorious here means splendid, arrayed; the picture is of a bride brought forward in full beauty, and the beauty is the bridegroom's gift. This is the church as she will be, not as she is, and the difference is the whole doctrine of sanctification running toward glorification. Paul is not describing a congregation any reader would recognise; he is describing what Christ is making. The passage is set inside instruction to husbands, and the logic runs from the greater to the lesser: husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it. A husband's self-giving is patterned on a love that takes full responsibility for what the beloved becomes.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a small ridge or prominence, or a furrow, formed by the shrinking or contraction of any smooth substance; a crease in the skin or in cloth.

expand to see more

WRINKLE, n. A small ridge or prominence, or a furrow, formed by the shrinking or contraction of any smooth substance.

WRINKLE, n. A crease or fold in the face or skin, usually the effect of age.

WRINKLE, v.t. To contract into furrows and prominences; to crease.

BLEMISH, n. Any mark of deformity; any scar or defect that diminishes beauty or renders imperfect.

PRESENT, v.t. To set, place or introduce into the presence of a superior; to exhibit to view.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 5:27 — "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish."

Ephesians 5:25 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;"

2 Peter 3:14 — "Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless."

Philippians 3:21 — "Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself."

Modern Corruption

The verse is used either to demand a perfectionism no congregation can produce or to justify indifference about the church's actual condition; Paul describes a work Christ is doing and will finish.

expand to see more

Perfectionist and separatist movements read Ephesians 5:27 as a present standard and then go looking for the spotless church, which does not exist; the search produces either endless division as each new body proves flawed, or the pretence that one's own assembly has arrived. The tense of the passage forbids it. Christ might present the church so — a purpose still being worked out, whose completion belongs to the day of glorification. The Reformed tradition has always held that the visible church in this world is mixed and imperfect, and Paul wrote these words to a congregation he had to correct at length.

The opposite error takes the promise as a reason for complacency: since Christ will present her spotless, her present condition matters little. But the same sentence names the means — he sanctifies and cleanses her now — and the New Testament everywhere presses the church toward what she is becoming. Peter draws exactly this inference: seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless. The certainty of the end is the motive for effort, not a substitute for it. And the image guards a doctrine about Christ as well as about the church, since a bridegroom who takes responsibility for his bride's beauty is the pattern Paul then hands to every husband.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek rhutis (G4512), a wrinkle; spilos (G4696), a spot or stain; paristemi (G3936), to present; amomos (G299), without blemish.

expand to see more

Greek rhutis (G4512) — a wrinkle, a fold; its only occurrence in Scripture.

Greek spilos (G4696) — a spot, a stain; the fault that comes from outside.

Greek paristemi (G3936) — to present, to set beside; a word used of presenting a bride.

Greek amomos (G299) — unblemished, faultless; used of the sacrificial lamb and of the church.

Greek endoxos (G1741) — glorious, splendid; the church as she will be presented.

Usage

"“not having spot, or wrinkle” — stain from without, crease from within."

"“that he might present it to himself” — the bridegroom does the adorning."

"“be diligent that ye may be found of him… without spot” — the inference Peter draws."
